stem: How many components make up the formal definition of a Turing machine?
explanation: A Turing machine is a 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, qaccept, qreject).

stem: Which of these can a Turing machine do that a finite automaton cannot?

options.text: Write on its tape as well as read
Move its head both left and right
Use an infinite tape as memory
Process input with a fixed number of states only

explanation: A TM reads and writes, moves both ways and has an infinite tape; a fixed set of states is all a finite automaton has.
source: CSC 552 Study Session 1, 1.3; CSC 552 Study Session 2, 2.2.1

stem: Every Turing-decidable language is Turing-recognisable, but not every Turing-recognisable language is decidable.
explanation: Recursive (decidable) languages are a subset of recursively enumerable (recognisable) languages.

stem: Given δ(q1, b) = (q2, c, L), what does the configuration aaq1bb yield?
explanation: The machine writes c over the b under the head and moves left, giving aq2acb.

stem: A Turing machine that halts on every input is called a
explanation: Turing machines that halt on all inputs are deciders because they always accept or reject.

stem: Which one is not a variant of the Turing machine described in the course?
explanation: A DFA is a weaker model; the other three are Turing machine variants with the same power.

stem: To simulate a nondeterministic TM, the deterministic TM should explore the computation tree depth-first.
explanation: Depth-first search could follow an infinite branch forever, so breadth-first search is used.

stem: Turing machine M2 decides the strings of 0s whose length is a power of 2. What does it do on each sweep?

options.text: Crosses off the first and last 0
Copies the 0s to a second tape

explanation: Each sweep crosses off every other 0, halving the count; it accepts at a single 0 and rejects an odd count above 1.
